_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/enforce and the suite must fail. F1 is the #29 fail-open: a session that reports itself locked used to be left alone, and LockedHint is writable by the child. See scripts/mutate.py for what the run checks and what equivalent means. Run: make mutate

SURVIVES BY DESIGN, and kept so the battery says so out loud. The race this mutant reproduces is a property of the test harness, not of the product: the goroutine unlocks a handful of instructions after the send, so the main goroutine's TryLock -- TryLock on purpose, because refusing a busy tick is the correct behaviour -- wins almost always. That is why the original flake was one CI run in several rather than a hard failure, and why no assertion in this test can observe the interval without artificially widening it. Measured at this head with the mutation applied exactly as defined: whole package -count=1 ok, GOMAXPROCS=1 -count=60 ok, -race -count=20 ok. The 240-failures-in-240-runs figure in the history was taken with the window widened, which is a statement about the widened harness and not something the shipped test can reproduce. Marked equivalent because no test in this set can distinguish it -- that is a statement about the guard's scope, not a claim the mutation is harmless. The ordering fix in run_test.go is still the right fix for the real flake; it is simply not a property a mutant can pin at this width. C3 in auth.json is the precedent for recording it this way.

prints the recovery line on every successful read instead of on the transition out of a stale period. This is the bug the live Plasma run caught: the daemon log said 'config readable again' on a machine that had never been stale, once per tick for the life of the process. e.cfg was assigned two lines above, so the extra term is simply always true.

deletes the recovery signal along with the false line. The transition has two directions and only the healthy one was wrong; the operator's only notice that a stretch of enforcement ran on stale rules has stopped is this line.

the startup line goes back to reading interval() before the first tick has published pollSeconds, so it quotes the compiled default whatever the config says. Measured on the dev loop: pollSeconds 5 printed 'every 30s'. The line exists to tell an operator whether they are waiting 5s or 5m, and it was telling them the wrong one
the unreadable-config branch quotes a period anyway, presenting a default as a measurement in the same breath the first tick is about to report the file as unreadable

startupPeriod answers 0 for an unreadable config instead of the negative sentinel, so the caller takes the 'we know the period' branch and prints 'every 0s' -- a number nobody configured, on the one line an operator trusts to time their wait

interval() accepts a published 0, and time.NewTimer fires immediately for a non-positive duration -- the enforcement loop spins, re-locking as fast as loginctl answers, on the tick that is supposed to be 30 seconds apart

the configured period is never published before the first timer is armed, so the loop's first wait is the compiled default whatever the config says -- measured as two lock calls 30s apart on a machine whose config said 5s and whose startup line correctly said 5s
the engine ignoring the self-session rule entirely: the daemon locks the session it is running in and can no longer be stopped. TestTheDaemonsOwnSessionIsNotLocked.

forgetting to record that the skip was announced, so a deployment mistake that never fixes itself emits one audit line every tick -- the volume #35 exists to prevent. TestTheOwnSessionIsAnnouncedOnceNotEveryTick.
saying it will not lock and then locking anyway: the return dropped, so the tick falls through to the lock. TestTheDaemonsOwnSessionIsNotLocked.

the diagnostic half of the account switch. Deleting it does NOT free the child -- config.ProfileFor refuses a disabled account too (CG14 is the mutant for that) -- but the release is filed as "no profile" and the tick emits "user is enabled but has no profile" every thirty seconds, so the one account the parent switched off on purpose is reported as a broken document. TestReEnablingAnAccountIsObeyedOnTheNextTick, TestSessionsThatMustNeverBeLockedAreLeftAlone.

the exit sweep runs after a census that is short, so an id missing from `seen` is guessed to be a logout when it is really the row that could not be read: lockout.exited for a child still sitting at a locked screen, and the state carrying their override bookkeeping deleted with it. Re-pointed from `if len(sessions) == 0 { return rep }`, which this PR made equivalent -- the guard below already returns on any error, so no mutant can distinguish that arm and the battery would have been reporting an equivalent as a catch. TestAPartialReadDoesNotEndALockoutItCouldNotSee, TestATotalFailureDoesNotEndALockout

the dismissal goes back to being invisible. #177 measured SetActive(false) on the child's own session bus clearing a password-gated lock with no password; the loop already re-asserts every poll, so the absorb works and, with this gone, nothing else says it happened -- an absorbed attack and a quiet night both write lock.asserted. TestAConfirmedLockThatComesBackIsReportedOnce.

the level instead of the transition: report whenever the hint says unlocked. A locker that corroborates without ever writing LockedHint is a healthy machine, so this accuses someone of tampering on every poll of it -- the alarm-on-a-quiet-box failure #35 already cost this package its cadence work. TestAReleaseIsNeverReportedForASessionThatNeverReportedLocked.

the transition is never consumed, so a screen left unlocked reports a fresh dismissal every thirty seconds for as long as it stays off. The flood is the point: it is what makes the first line unread. TestAConfirmedLockThatComesBackIsReportedOnce.

the rule is never armed, so no release is ever reportable even though the transition still happens. Reads as a quieter trail and nothing else: the lock is still re-asserted, the hint is still read, and the audit file goes back to saying lock.asserted forever. TestAConfirmedLockThatComesBackIsReportedOnce.

the exemption path keeps the release bookkeeping. An override hands the child their desktop back on purpose, so the first poll after it expires reports the parent's own grant as the child dismissing a lock -- the one false accusation this line cannot afford, because it is the line a parent acts on. This is the one release path where the state entry survives, which is why the reset has to be here and not only in the delete on the exit path. TestAnOverrideDoesNotReportTheParentsOwnGrantAsADismissal.
